evals.prompt: We run Google Search ads for Corvid Systems, a B2B compliance software company. We get about 9 demo-request conversions a month from search, at roughly $370 per demo, on a $120/day budget. Our new agency says we have to stay on manual CPC until we hit 15 conversions in a 30-day window because that's Google's requirement for Target CPA, and ideally 50 before it works properly. Is the agency right, and what should we do in the meantime?
evals.expected_output: Corrects the threshold folklore (Target CPA has no conversion minimum; 15/30d belongs to Target ROAS; 50 is guidance), reframes low volume as a variance problem, derives what the budget can support, and lays out ranked options for thin volume with a trailing-actual starting target.
expectations: States that the cost-goal strategy (Google Target CPA) has no documented minimum conversion volume and can be started with no conversion history
Attributes the '15 conversions in 30 days' minimum to Target ROAS (the return-goal strategy), not to Target CPA
Identifies '50 conversions' figures as reliability recommendations or guidance, not enablement gates
Distinguishes enablement thresholds from evaluation samples as two different kinds of published number that folklore merges
Does not advise waiting until 15 or 50 conversions before adopting Target CPA
States that low conversion volume costs variance and slow diagnosis (a bad target cannot be separated from bad luck), not eligibility or access
Applies the volume-budget derivation (required budget ≈ target cost × volume threshold ÷ period) to the account's own numbers, e.g. showing what $120/day at ~$370 supports
Presents consolidation, optimizing an upstream event with downstream outcome import, and accepting slower diagnosis as the options for thin volume
Ranks those thin-volume options rather than listing them flat, with consolidation leading on efficiency
Notes that importing downstream outcomes requires consent/privacy/legal review before customer or deal data is sent to a platform
Recommends setting the initial Target CPA at or near the trailing actual (~$370), not at a goal or aspirational number
Labels cited thresholds with an evidence tier or as-of date, or advises re-verifying them against live platform documentation
Treats manual CPC as a durable strategy with legitimate long-term uses rather than dismissing it as only a bootstrapping phase

evals.prompt: I manage Meta ads for Loam & Ember, a DTC candle brand. Three weeks ago I set a Cost Per Result Goal of $28 on our main purchase campaign. Looking at individual purchases in the export, several cost $47 and one even $63. The average across the campaign is $29.50. This looks broken to me - the whole point of the setting is that results stay under $28, right? I'm about to open a support ticket, or switch to Bid Cap at $28 so Meta actually respects the number. Which should I do?
evals.expected_output: Explains average-based control vs hard per-auction ceiling, concludes the campaign is working as designed, and warns against the Bid Cap swap and the learning reset it would trigger.
expectations: Explains that Cost Per Result Goal is an average-based control: individual conversions can and will exceed the target while the average lands near it
Concludes the campaign is working as designed (average $29.50 near the $28 target), not malfunctioning
Does not endorse opening a support ticket or the bug framing
Distinguishes average-based cost goals from hard per-auction ceilings as two structurally different control types
Identifies Bid Cap as the hard per-auction ceiling that never bids above the cap in any single auction
Warns that a hard cap at $28 carries under-delivery risk (delivery can drop sharply)
Notes that platforms position hard bid caps as expert-only controls
States this misreading ('my cost cap was exceeded') is a common conflation rather than a rare malfunction
Does not recommend switching to Bid Cap as the fix for the observed spread
Warns that a strategy switch is a material change that restarts a learning period
Advises judging the target over an evaluation window expressed in conversion cycles, not on individual conversions
Treats the platform label as an observed capability (noting label churn such as Cost Cap being renamed) rather than assuming the name describes a hard cap

evals.prompt: Finance at Pellwright, our B2B payroll software company, set next quarter's plan around a $95 cost per demo. Our trailing 60-day actual is $240 per demo, and the best month we've ever had was $210. Last Tuesday I changed our search campaign's target from $240 to $95, and since then spend has dropped almost to zero while the platform reports a beautiful $102 CPA on the trickle that's left. Finance says the target is working and we should keep it. For context: a closed deal is worth about $3,500 in contribution and roughly 4% of demos become customers. What do I do?
evals.expected_output: Diagnoses a target-choke delivery collapse, computes break-even at $140, declares economics and history irreconcilable (unit-economics problem, not a bidding problem), restores the target to trailing actual, and sets change discipline.
expectations: Diagnoses the spend collapse as a target-too-aggressive delivery choke: the platform stops bidding rather than lose money
Identifies the reported ~$102 CPA on near-zero spend as the signature symptom of the choke (under-delivery with great-looking reported efficiency), not as success
Names the discriminating under-delivery signals to check, such as spend well below budget or impression share lost to rank
Computes break-even cost per demo as $3,500 × 4% = $140
Compares the $140 break-even against the $210-240 achieved history and states the account has never operated at or below break-even
Declares this a unit-economics problem (offer, pricing, funnel conversion, or channel fit), not a bidding problem
Refuses to pursue the $95 target through any bid-strategy change
Recommends restoring the target to or near the trailing actual ($240) to recover delivery
Recommends tightening only in modest steps (about 10-15%), labelled as practitioner convention rather than platform documentation
Requires a full evaluation window between steps, expressed in conversion cycles
Names or quantifies a margin buffer between break-even and the live target
Corrects finance's reading rather than endorsing 'the target is working'
Attaches a refresh cadence or date to the derived inputs (e.g. re-derive the close rate from CRM actuals quarterly)

evals.prompt: Velora Home, our e-commerce store, does a big Black Friday-Cyber Monday sale - conversions usually triple that weekend, and November overall runs hot compared to October. My plan: apply a +200% seasonality adjustment in Google Ads for all of November, and add a data exclusion over the sale weekend itself so learning doesn't get polluted by the unusual data. We also run 25% off sitewide during the sale. Sanity-check this before I set it up?
evals.expected_output: Resizes the adjustment to conversion-rate lift, limits the spike tool to the short event window, re-derives the seasonal target for the month-long pattern, rejects data exclusions for demand swings, and flags the discount's effect on margin-derived targets.
expectations: Sizes the seasonality adjustment to the expected conversion-rate lift, not the conversion-count multiple
Explains that conversions tripling does not mean conversion rate triples, since traffic also rises during the sale
Warns an oversized adjustment causes overspend or budget exhaustion early in the day
Restricts the seasonality-adjustment tool to a short event window (roughly 1-7 days), not a full month
For the month-long November pattern, recommends re-deriving the target from seasonal actuals instead of stretching the spike tool
Rejects using data exclusions for a demand swing
States data exclusions exist for broken or corrupted tracking, not unusual demand
Warns that frequent data exclusions degrade the bidder
Recommends restoring normal targets/settings after the sale window ends
Distinguishes a temporary demand swing (loosen, then restore) from a permanent efficiency change (re-derive the target permanently)
Flags that the 25% sitewide discount changes contribution margin and therefore the break-even/target derivation for the promo period
Advises against other concurrent target changes during the promo window

evals.prompt: Our CEO at Brightquay, a marketplace for boat rentals, read that eBay proved brand search ads are a waste because organic picks up the clicks anyway, and he wants all brand bidding stopped this week. Meanwhile our retargeting campaigns show a 5.8x ROAS, the best in the account, and he wants that budget doubled instead. Our agency says brand always pays. Who's right, and what do I tell him?
evals.expected_output: Refuses both blanket positions, frames eBay as an upper bound against the opposing replication, prescribes a holdout/geo incrementality test for brand and retargeting alike, and moves scaling decisions to marginal rather than average return.
expectations: Refuses both blanket positions (stop all brand bidding, and 'brand always pays')
Frames the eBay finding as an upper bound driven by exceptional brand strength, not a general law
Cites the replication that found the opposite (Edmunds: substitution under 50%, paid brand traffic economically meaningful)
States the operative instruction as 'test, don't assume'
Recommends a holdout or geo test as the way to detect non-incremental buying
Explains that a bidder rewarded on attributed conversions will buy conversions that would have happened anyway
States a strategy can perform well against its own objective while destroying money (platform metrics healthy, lift near zero)
Applies the same incrementality gate to retargeting before doubling its budget, treating the 5.8x attributed ROAS as unproven lift
Advises scaling decisions on marginal return, not average return
Notes average return can hold high while the marginal return on the next dollar sits below break-even
Requires incrementality or attribution measurement before any budget move rather than deciding this week from platform reporting alone

evals.prompt: Halden Grove Software sells facilities-management software to universities. Six months ago we moved our search campaigns to automated bidding on demo-request form fills. Cost per form fill is down 30% and volume is up, but our SDR team says most of the new leads are students and job seekers, not facilities directors. Half the marketing team wants to go back to manual bidding because the algorithm is a black box we can't trust; the other half says never fight the machine. Sales cycle is about 4 months. How should we settle this?
evals.expected_output: Applies Vallaeys' Pilot/Doctor/Teacher framework, diagnoses a failing Teacher job (junk signal), fixes the optimization event and offline loop before touching the strategy, and rejects the manual revert while layering monitoring on the bidder.
expectations: Applies the automation-layering framework of the three human jobs: Pilot, Doctor, and Teacher
Attributes the framework to Frederick Vallaeys (or Optmyzr)
Reframes the manual-vs-automated debate into which of the three jobs the account is currently failing
Diagnoses this account as failing the Teacher job: junk conversion signal feeding the bidder
States the fix is the signal/optimization event, not the bid strategy
States that an improving cost per form fill alongside junk leads means the tracked event is wrong, not the bidder
Does not recommend reverting to manual bidding as the remedy
Requires measurement repair (a deeper funnel event or offline outcome import) before any bidding change
Identifies closing the offline loop - pushing CRM stage outcomes with real deal values back to the platform - as the highest-impact B2B move
Recommends matching the conversion window to the ~4-month sales cycle rather than platform defaults
Recommends monitoring rules layered on top of the automated bidder as a complement, not a competition
Acknowledges legitimate durable homes for manual bidding (e.g. brand-defense terms, tiny audiences) while rejecting them as grounds in this case

evals.prompt: Tinderbox Apparel is a DTC clothing brand. Our premium line runs about a 55% contribution margin, our basics line about 22%, and blended it's roughly 40%. Our new agency wants one account-wide target ROAS of 4x because that's the industry standard for e-commerce. We're currently at 2.6x trailing 30 days, and the founder wants 10% net profit on ad-driven revenue. Purchase values flow back server-side. What target should we actually set?
evals.expected_output: Derives break-even ROAS from margin instead of accepting 4x, splits the blended target by margin band, starts at trailing actual and tightens toward the profit-goal number with a named buffer, refund netting, and a refresh trigger.
expectations: Rejects 4x as an industry standard: break-even return depends on margin, not convention
States or shows that the folk 4x figure is correct specifically for a 25%-margin business
Computes blended break-even ROAS as 1 ÷ 0.40 = 2.5x
Computes per-line break-evens (premium ≈ 1.8x, basics ≈ 4.5x)
Flags that one blended target averages a high-margin and a near-break-even line into one meaningless number
Recommends splitting the policy or campaign structure by margin band before tightening
Applies the profit-goal form 1 ÷ (margin − desired net margin) = 1 ÷ 0.30 ≈ 3.3x as the tightening destination
Sets the initial target at trailing actual (2.6x), not at 4x or the 3.3x goal
For a return target, starts at or slightly below trailing actual (the looser-than-achieved direction)
Names the margin buffer between the live target and blended break-even (~0.1x) and flags it as thin
Tightens toward the profit-goal number in modest steps with a full evaluation window per step
Requires values net of refunds (or checks refund materiality) before trusting a return target
Attaches a margin refresh trigger: re-derive on any pricing change and at least quarterly

evals.prompt: I run marketing at Ferrostat, a B2B industrial-sensors company. On Google Search we have three campaigns: branded (120 conversions/month), competitor prospecting (14/month), and a generic demand campaign (9/month). Our agency proposes one portfolio Target ROAS across all three so the small campaigns can learn from the big one. They also want to mirror value-based bidding on our LinkedIn campaigns using deal values from Salesforce. Nothing flows from the CRM to either platform yet. Green-light both?
evals.expected_output: Runs the pooling compatibility test and rejects mixing brand with prospecting, blocks any return-goal until real values flow and legal review clears, and states LinkedIn offers no value-based bidding at all.
expectations: Applies the pooling compatibility test before any portfolio: same conversion event, comparable margins, same target
Rejects pooling the brand campaign with prospecting campaigns
Explains that pooled spend migrates on blended rather than per-campaign returns, distorting allocation when economics differ
Acknowledges pooling legitimately helps thin campaigns clear signal floors when the pooled goals are genuinely compatible
Names the diagnostic for pooling gone wrong: blended target looks fine while per-campaign returns diverge, so incompatible campaigns get split out
Suggests consolidation as the alternative fix for structurally thin campaigns
States that LinkedIn does not offer value-based / return-goal bidding
Treats bidding capabilities as observed per platform rather than assuming feature parity across platforms
Notes Google's return-goal (Target ROAS) carries a documented minimum for Search (15 conversions in the past 30 days) with an as-of or re-verify caveat
Blocks any return-goal recommendation until real differentiated values actually flow back, since nothing flows from the CRM yet
Requires legal/privacy/consent review before Salesforce deal values are sent to any platform
Runs the value-integrity check (values differentiated, net of refunds/rejects, timely relative to lag) as a prerequisite
Notes the 9-14 conversion/month campaigns clear no documented return-goal minimum on their own

evals.prompt: Over the last two weeks at Nockboard, our B2B webinar platform, I've adjusted our Meta cost per result goal three times ($60 to $48 to $55 to $50), refreshed the creative, and narrowed the audience, because results kept swinging. It's still volatile. Typical lag from click to a qualified signup is about 3 weeks, plus a few days before it shows in reporting. I want to write down bidding rules so the team stops improvising - including an automated rule that pauses any ad set above $90 CPA. Can you draft the rules?
evals.expected_output: Diagnoses learning churn, freezes edits and batches changes, defines the window in conversion cycles converted to this account's ~3.5-week lag, refuses the hardcoded auto-pause rule, and drafts a policy with rollback trigger, switch trigger, and named approver, validated section by section.
expectations: Diagnoses learning churn: each edit re-enters a learning period, and the induced instability provoked the next edit
Instructs to stop editing and wait out a full window before any further change
Requires batching pending changes into a single change to trigger one relearn instead of a chain of resets
Prohibits concurrent confounding changes (target, creative, and audience moved in the same week)
Defines the evaluation window in conversion cycles (click-to-conversion lag plus reporting delay), not calendar days
Converts the window to days for this account (one cycle ≈ 3.5 weeks, so 1-2 cycles ≈ 4-7 weeks)
Cites vendor guidance of 1-2 conversion cycles after a target change as the documented unit
Refuses the hardcoded auto-pause rule based on a fixed CPA threshold alone
Lists the checks required before pausing on a spike: conversion lag, sample size, tracking health, seasonality, active experiments
States that a cost spike is a question, not a verdict
Names the containment exception (runaway spend, policy exposure, broken destination, confirmed tracking corruption) where an immediate hold is right
Drafts the policy with a rollback trigger stated as an observable condition
Includes a switch trigger and a named approver in the drafted rules
Presents the policy sections for the user's validation/approval rather than finalizing unilaterally

evals.prompt: Cindercart runs both a shopping app and a web store. Our app UA agency reports ROAS at 160% and calls it strong; our web team reports 4.2x and calls the app numbers a disaster in comparison. Meanwhile our Google reps are pushing us to move most of the web budget into Performance Max, and my boss's take is that it's just another campaign type, so flip it on. Two questions: which team is actually performing better, and do we do the PMax move?
evals.expected_output: Normalizes the ROAS unit conventions before comparing (160% = 1.6x vs 4.2x), then evaluates Performance Max adoption as delegating the whole bidding policy - signal given, control surrendered, written exit criterion, guardrails, and a clean conversion signal first.
expectations: Normalizes the ROAS units before comparing: mobile-UA tooling reports a percentage, web platforms report a multiplier
Converts 160% to 1.6x and compares like units (making the web store's 4.2x materially ahead on reported figures)
Warns that comparing the two conventions raw produces a large misread
Treats adopting Performance Max as delegating the bidding policy to the platform, not as a campaign-type checkbox
Notes AI-default campaign types use automated bidding exclusively, so adoption is itself the bid-strategy decision
Asks or answers what signal the platform gets under the delegation
Asks or answers what control is given up by delegating
Requires a written exit criterion: what would justify taking control back
Requires guardrails and exclusions configured before adoption
Requires a clean, valid conversion signal as a precondition for delegating
Recommends cross-checking platform-attributed return against MER or blended business revenue before trusting either team's number
